Under color of law expression is not explicitly embossed in the law, though the concept is there. So, for brevity' s sake I took the liberty of using an expression US citizens would be familiar with.

The typical idea is the same, though under European Treaty law, three main perspectives for a law to be lawful need to be observed: effective to obtain it' s purpose, proportionality and subsidiarity, in that order. meaning:

A law may serve a purpose of say, limit civil liberties to protect citizens to come into harms way when flooding, war, civil disturbance, civil war, or any other act of God may occur. Usually, these measures are local and in very rare instances national. Think curfew, or a limitation on the number and locality of a protest. A law may have an unintended consequence, and may need remedial action. But that does no immediately mean the law would be unlawful.

When such a law is deemed effective, it does not mean it is proportional. Meaning, is the risk perceived really there? And if such a risk were to manifest, does it affect every locality at every time in equal measure.

Even if that were to be the case, say a stay home order were to be mandated, subsidiarity considers whether the object of a measure or law can be achieved by less intrusive measures.

In the case of Masks, the law to mandate it may be perceived to limit the transmission risk of a virus. Whether that is so, is a matter of technicality, not law. A peer reviewed representative study may support such an idea or not. In reality, it does not. Therefore, the measure is unlawful.

The laying on fines for not wearing a mask may be deemed effective since no one wants to pay the fare or risk a criminal record.

Proportional: is the measure of wearing masks fitting for the perceived risk. This is an answer that also relies heavily on scientific knowledge, and is somewhat confusing. A clothmask does not help. A N95 mask may help. To mandate the wearing of a mask, lest one is cited for 90 Euro' s and a criminal record is hardly proportional, since the measure does not work and has therefore no relation to the object of preventing spread. (concept of aerosolized virus through droplets in breadth)

Subsidiarity: Can the object of the mandate, the prevention of spread, be reached by a less intrusive measure?

That is a somewhat difficult question to answer since the object is the prevention of spread. It may be argued that sitting in a building or transport with climate management, the spread is actually promoted. So, should public transport be prohibited? Probably. Is the spread prevented by social distance? No.

In matter of questioning the legality of a law or measure, the mandate is wearing a mask. So the answer is: there is no known less intrusive alternative. Hence, it is unlawful to mandate.

The same type of reasoning can be applied to the connection between citation and criminal record. Although a citation may be warranted, a criminal record would be very intrusive and does fail of subsidiarity. In terms of proportionality, this has to be seen in light of the perceived risk. It may have been proportional when one would go with the Imperial College models and when there was less information available, but today .... that would be a hard case to demonstrate.
